∡(a, b) is the directed angle between the lines a and b: the angle through which line a must be turned counter-clockwise to become parallel to b, taken modulo 180°; ∡XYZ means ∡(YX, YZ). These are angles between lines, not ordinary angles: 0° and 180° are the same directed angle, so their equalities are written ≡ … (mod 180°). Write A, B, C for the angles of triangle ABC and R = OA = OB = OC for its circumradius. Write D, E, F for the angles of triangle DEF. Let Ω be the circumcircle of triangle ABC, with center O; S lies on Ω. Let ω₁ be the circle (DEF); G lies on ω₁. Let U be a point other than A on the perpendicular from A to BC. Let V be a point other than D on the parallel to EF through D. Let X be the midpoint of BC. Let Y be the foot of the perpendicular from A to BC. Let Z be the reflection of H in BC. Let W be the reflection of A in O. Let L be the circumcenter of △ABH. Let M be the orthocenter of △ABC. Let N be the incenter of △ABC. Let T be the excenter of △ABC opposite A. Let X be an excenter of △ABC. Let Y be the centroid of △ABC. Let Z be the foot of the bisector from A in △ABC. Let W be the antipode of A on Ω. Let L be the antipode of D on ω₁. Let M be the point such that ABCM is a parallelogram. Let N be the point where the incircle of △ABC touches the side opposite A. Let T be the point where the excircle of △ABC opposite A touches the side opposite A. Let X be the center of the spiral similarity taking AB to CD. Let Y be the isogonal conjugate of P in △ABC. Let Z be the inverse of P in Ω. Let W be the pole of line BC with respect to Ω. Let L be the point of contact of a tangent from P to the circle (Q, QD). Let M be the midpoint of arc BC of Ω. Let N be the harmonic conjugate of D with respect to B and C. Let T be the intersection of the parallel to BC through D and AB. Let X be the intersection of the perpendicular to AC through H and the tangent at A to the circle centered at O. Let Y be the intersection of the isogonal of AP in ∠BAC and BC. Let Z be the second intersection of line AD with Ω. Let W be the second intersection of Ω with the circle (Q, QD).

Plan: it suffices to show that ∡ABX ≡ ∡XCA (mod 180°).

1. We show that ∡ABX ≡ ∡XCA (mod 180°):

∡ABX ≡ ∡ACX    [inscribed angles in Ω]
     ≡ ∡XCA (mod 180°)    [inscribed angles in (ABCX)] (1)

2. We show that AB ⟂ CX:

∡DEG ≡ ∡DFG    [∡DEG ≡ ∡DFG (mod 180°)]
     ≡ ∡QDE + 90° (mod 180°)    [QD = QE = QF = QG; radii of Ω; HA = HB = HC; KA = KB = KC; AY is tangent to Ω (tangent–chord angle)]

D, E, F, G on ω₁, so ∡DEG ≡ ∡DFG (mod 180°). ∡ABX ≡ ∡XCA (mod 180°), by (1), so AB ⟂ CX, as required. Apply the law of sines in △ABC. Apply the law of sines in △DEF (DE ⟂ EF). Law of sines in △ABC and sin∠AXB = sin C, so AB = 2R·sin C. D, E, F, G on ω₁, so ∡EDF ≡ ∡EGF (mod 180°).

∠DEG = 180° − ∠GEK    [D, E, K collinear: supplementary angles]
     = ∠LEM    [vertical angles at E]
     = ∠DFG    [exterior angle of the cyclic quadrilateral EDFG]
     = 180° − ∠DSG    [opposite angles of the cyclic quadrilateral FDSG]
     = ∠XDY    [the tangent at D is ⟂ OD (tangent–chord angle)]
     = ∠ZDY    [common angle at D]

∠DEG = ∠DFG and E, F lie on the same side of DG, so by the converse of the inscribed angle theorem, D, E, F, G are concyclic. ∠DFG + ∠DSG = 180° and F, S lie on opposite sides of DG, so by the converse of the opposite-angle theorem for cyclic quadrilaterals, D, F, G, S are concyclic. ∠GEK = ∠DFG and E, F lie on opposite sides of DG, so by the converse of the exterior-angle theorem for cyclic quadrilaterals, D, E, F, G are concyclic. D, E, F, G on ω₁ and D, F, G, S concyclic; these circles share three points, so they coincide and D, E, F, G, S are concyclic. DE : DF = AB : AC, so DE / DF = AB / AC. DE = AB, so △DEF ≅ △ABC (similar by AA, with equal corresponding sides). K is the reflection of H in BC, so BC is the perpendicular bisector of HK; hence BC ⟂ HK. A, H, K collinear and H lies on the segment KA, so ∠HKB = ∠AKB. AH ∥ OM, so ∠GAH = ∠AMO (alternate angles).

∠MCA = ∠BAE    [CM ∥ AB; corresponding angles]
     = ∠AMC    [angle sum in △MAC]

∠BFA = 90° and ∠BNA = 90°, so by the converse of Thales' theorem, F, N, B, A are concyclic. Common side AB, so △ABM ≅ △ABE (similar by AA, with equal corresponding sides). ∎
